<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">With recent advancements in video backbone architectures, combined with the remarkable achievements of large language models (LLMs), the analysis of long-form videos spanning tens of minutes has become both feasible and increasingly prevalent. However, the inherently redundant nature of video sequences poses significant challenges for contemporary state-of-the-art models. These challenges stem from two primary aspects: 1) efficiently incorporating a larger number of frames within memory constraints, and 2) extracting discriminative information from the vast volume of input data. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end schema for long-form video understanding, which includes an information-density-based adaptive video sampler (AVS) and an autoencoder-based spatiotemporal video compressor (SVC) integrated with a multimodal large language model (MLLM). Our proposed system offers two major advantages: it adaptively and effectively captures essential information from video sequences of varying durations, and it achieves high compression rates while preserving crucial discriminative information. The proposed framework demonstrates promising performance across various benchmarks, excelling in both long-form video understanding tasks and standard video understanding benchmarks. These results underscore the versatility and efficacy of our approach, particularly in managing the complexities of prolonged video sequences.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<blockquote id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">”The whole is greater than the sum of its parts.”</span></p>
<p id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_right">— Aristotle</p><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:198.7pt;height:0.4pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>
</blockquote>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17869v1/fig1.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:685/623;" width="685" height="623" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An overview of our method and previous works, showing the different way of modeling long-form video with LLM. Specifically, (a) interpret clip into clip-level caption and aggregate via LLM in the linguistic space, (b) uniformly sample the video frame and leverage paired text to compress video tokens, and (c) our proposed method that leverage adaptive video sampler (AVS) and autoencoder based spatiotemporal video compressor (SVC).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Long-form video understanding has emerged as a hot topic in the research community, presenting significant challenges due to its complexity and dynamic nature, and remains an unsolved problem despite ongoing advancements. Conventional approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> often focus on classification tasks, where the goal is to map an entire video to one or a few predefined ground truth labels. These methods typically treat the video as a single, unified entity, aiming to assign a label that best represents the overall content. Although effective in some contexts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, these approaches are insufficient to understand long-form video, as they do not capture the complexity and contextual relationships unfolded across multiple scenes over time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> have made a significant impact on the field of video understanding, showcasing remarkable emergent capabilities across a variety of video-related tasks, such as perception, common sense reasoning, and open dialogue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite>. However, many of these models face challenges in effectively learning and modeling long-form video. This difficulty arises from the redundant nature of video sequences, which often results in an overwhelming number of visual tokens, leading to substantial computational overhead in LLMs. RoPe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite> provides a solution to handle the extended context during inference. However, the complexity of a long-form video sequence requires a more effective encoding solution during training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, one successful attempt <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, illustrated in Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A.2 Adaptive Frame Sampler ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (a), is to represent the long-video hierarchy with the natural language, which segments the long video sequences into several short clips and produces video segment captions. These short captions are subsequently fed into the LLMs for inference. However, these models interpret video clips into natural languages in the early stage, leading to the loss of much low-level visual information. Additionally, aggregated hallucinations from segment-level captions may result in poor generalizability and performance across various tasks and models. Another direction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> focuses on reducing the large number of tokens in long-form videos by introducing a learnable compression or token merging module, or a memory bank linked to the LLM, as shown in Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A.2 Adaptive Frame Sampler ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (b). However, scaling these methods is challenging, as they require a large volume of video-text pairs, with the linguistic information serving as guidance for training the compressor. Finally, parameter-free pooling operations (such as average pooling) have been proven effective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, but information loss remains unavoidable and is even more severe in long-form videos, where the diversity within video sequences is greater than in short videos.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive schema for long-form video understanding, covering the entire pipeline, from sampling to compression to high-level interpretation. This system includes: 1) an Adaptive Video Sampler (AVS) that selects video frames based on information density, 2) an Auto-Encoder based <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite> Spatiotemporal Video Compressor (SVC) that can be effectively trained with video-only data, and 3) a MLLM that integrates seamlessly with both the compressor and sampler. The AVS works jointly with SVC delivering 64-time compression to save the token budget for MLLMs. An overview of our proposed system is illustrated in Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A.2 Adaptive Frame Sampler ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (c). Our approach significantly reduces the token budget by 64 times, enabling MLLMs to process hours-long video sequences in their entirety. The proposed AVS and SVC modules ensure a sufficient capture of discriminative information while considerably expanding the perception field of the MLLM in long-form videos.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We conducted extensive experiments in a diverse range of tasks and problem settings to evaluate the proposed method. Our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various video benchmark downstream tasks while demonstrating superior efficiency by using substantially fewer visual tokens and reducing computational overhead. Notably, our method surpasses Llava-OV <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> by 2.6% and 3.3% on the EgoSchema and PercepTest tasks, respectively, while utilizing 80% fewer visual tokens. Our contributions are as follows.</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We proposed a novel long-form video understanding schema to equip MLLM, which includes two novel components: Adaptive Video Sampler (AVS) which samples frames based on the information density, and Spatio-temporal Video Compressor (SVC) that is an AE-based video compressor.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The proposed AVS and SVC work jointly to deliver 64-time compression ratio, which significantly save the token budget in MLLM while preserving the discriminative information of the long-form videos.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to baseline and competitive counterparts, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed elements and achieve performance on par with the SoTA methods in various video understanding benchmarks, while only utilizing 20% video tokens compared to the previous SoTA method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>MLLMs in Long-form videos</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast to conventional long-form video understanding tasks that classify entire long video as one or a few ground truth labels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) interpret long-form video within a well-defined linguistic space, thus expanding the scope of video understanding to include tasks such as contextual reasoning, open-ended dialogue about video content, and complex question-answering across long-video sequences.
However, the high computational cost of transformer-based LLMs poses a significant barrier to effectively processing entire sequences of long-form videos within memory constraints. To address this issue, one solution is to divide the entire long-form video into short clips and generate clip-level captions, which will be hierarchically aggregated as long-form video representation via LLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>. However, these models often lose significant low-level visual information, and the accumulated hallucinations from segment-level captions can lead to poor generalizability and reduced performance across various tasks and models. To this end, an efficient and effective video encoding scheme is required in long-form video understanding tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Long-form Video Encoding</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Token Reduction</span> Token reduction is one of the most effective methods to relieve computational burden. It can be further categorized as <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1) Token Selection</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2) Token Merging</span> and <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">3) Token Compression</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Token Selection</span>: Token selection is a common strategy for improving model efficiency, utilizing lightweight modules to retain only the most ”useful” tokens while discarding those considered less essential. Typical works, such as STTS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, AdaViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> and similar methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite> introduce a selection mechanism to assign importance scores to each token and selects the top-K important ones. However, it is impractical for a lightweight selection module to select discriminative information from a large volume of long-form video data without risking a loss of contextual information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Token Merging</span>: Originally proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, token merging is designed to enhance throughput in vision transformers without the need for further training. The merging technique splits visual tokens into two equal groups; for each token on the edge of one group, it identifies the closest matching token in the other group, merges them using average pooling, and then recombines the groups. Although this method is effective and straightforward, its use has been mainly limited to the image and short video domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. This is due to the high diversity in long-form videos, which often leads to mismatches in a similarity-based merging system. More practically, a sliding window-based averaging pooling cubic is widely adapted in recent long-form video understanding works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. In particular, Video-ChatGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> and SlowFast-LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> employ two distinct pooling strategies across spatial and temporal dimensions to capture object and motion information, respectively. However, these pooling strategies treat each video frame equally, which may result in information distortion when two dissimilar candidates are combined. Effectively reducing redundant visual tokens while preserving key information remains a challenge and further exploration is needed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Token Compression</span>: Recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite> have successfully leveraged a compressor to reduce the number of visual tokens while preserving useful information in various applications, such as classification, generation, and general understanding with LLMs. For example, Wiles et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite> leverage the VQ-VAE encoder-decoder model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> to apply augmentations
directly on the latent codes of compressed video and use them for classification tasks. Yu et al. propose MAGVIT-v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, which generates concise and expressive tokens for both videos and images utilizing a shared VQ-VAE codebook. In the field of long-form video understanding, MovieChat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> introduces a recurrent memory bank to consolidate excessive video tokens, while LLaMA-VID <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> uses cross attention to represent each video frame as two tokens. Furthermore, LongVU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> utilizes DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> features to eliminate redundant frames that exhibit high similarity. These works either rely on external prior or well-structured video and text pairs, which may easily introduce bias or prevent the algorithm scaling up. In this work, we argue that the token reduction mechanism should be implemented as a holistic pipeline that jointly considers video sampling and compression problems as a whole. To this end, we propose a simple yet effective adaptive video sampler as well as a video compressor that delivers a 64-time compression ratio over long-form video while preserving discriminative information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Video Backbone</span> Recently, Mamba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> and its huge family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> received promising results in various long context modeling tasks. Specifically, it utilizes a state-space sequence model with a structured convolutional kernel to efficiently capture long-context information, achieving linear complexity. However, stringent initialization conditions make it difficult for Mamba to be trained in large scale with MLLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. As a result, we follow previous works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> by using ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> as the video backbone. The exploration of Mamba with MLLMs will be left for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17869v1/fig2.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/269;" width="685" height="269" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of the proposed method.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminaries</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MLLM For Long-form Video Understanding
<br class="ltx_break"></span>Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) process vision data using LLMs to interpret visual information extracted from inputs alongside task-specific text prompts (e.g., visual questions about visual content), ultimately generating the corresponding responses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To be specific, given an input video <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> as an example, a set of frames, denoted as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math>, are first <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">uniformly</span> sampled form it. A pretrained visual encoder <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> then extracts visual token embeddings, denoted as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, from these sampled frames:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f=\mathcal{E}(X),\quad f\in\mathcal{R}^{T\times H\times W\times C}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f=\mathcal{E}(X),\quad f\in\mathcal{R}^{T\times H\times W\times C}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> represents the frame number, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> are height and width of the extracted feature tensor, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The LLM subsequently processes the visual tokens with the text question (<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>) to generate the answer <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=LLM(P(f),Q)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=LLM(P(f),Q)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> is a projector, such as the MLP module, that maps visual token features into the input space of the LLM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">However, in the context of long-form video, the volume of <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> increases significantly, which impacts the capacity of MLLM <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            The complexity of transformer-based LLMs is quadratic in relation to input length.</span></span></span> in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness. Additionally, uniform sampling combined with standard average pooling is suboptimal for long-form video, as redundant and irrelevant frames may consume the limited token budget of LLMs, ultimately reducing their ability to capture complex long-term dependencies. Motivated by these, we propose a long-form video understanding framework in this work, offering solutions and best practices for the research community.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Proposed Framework</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose a novel long-form video understanding framework, addressing the aforementioned challenges, from frame loading strategy to video token compression technique. Our framework consists of an Adaptive Video Sampler (AVS), a ViT-based video encoder, an autoencoder-based Spatiotemporal Video Compressor (SVC) and the recent popular LLM, QWen2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite>. An illustration is provided in Figure <a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ A.2 Adaptive Frame Sampler ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Adaptive Video Sampling</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In long-form videos, the discriminative information is not evenly distributed. Given the tight token budget of LLMs, it is important to carefully pick visual tokens from the entire sequence. To this end, we propose an information-density-based frame sampler that can adaptively select informative video frames from a long video sequence. We follow the decomposition rule of a movie, borrowing the concept of chapter, scene, and shot in the movie. It is assumed that each long-video sequence consists of serval continues information tubelets, with intra-tubelet information being generally homogeneous, while inter-tubelet data distributions vary significantly. As a result, the gradient of information shifts is crucial for identifying where discriminative information lies in the long-form video. In this work, we employ a shot boundary detection module as a core component of our adaptive frame sampler to capture dynamic moments that contain key information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, we first feed the entire video <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> to a shot boundary detector <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, which outputs a confidence score that indicates the likelihood of a content change with respect to each frame:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=\mathcal{S_{D}}(V),\quad S=\{s_{1},s_{2},...,s_{N}\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=\mathcal{S_{D}}(V),\quad S=\{s_{1},s_{2},...,s_{N}\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the confidence score for the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th frame, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of frames.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We then apply the non-maximum suppression (NMS) scheme to filter out redundant detections:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{\prime}=\mathrm{NMS}(S)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>NMS</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{\prime}=\mathrm{NMS}(S)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we sample frames with the top-k highest confidence scores and sort them temporally for video understanding:</p>

<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> represent the index of sampled frames</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Autoencoder-based Video Compressor</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the smart sampling strategy, the perception field of LLMs is still constrained by the massive number of visual tokens per frame. In the area of image and short-form videos, average pooling is widely used as an effective way to reduce redundant tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. However, it is argued that the average pooling is not ideal in long-form video understanding, as the high diversity among sparsely sampled frames can lead to information distortion when forced into aggregation. Unlike previous works that rely on knowledge priors or well-aligned video-text pairs to compress video tokens, we propose an autoencoder-based video compressor in this work. This compressor condenses raw video feature representations into a compact latent space, reducing the number of visual tokens while retaining essential information. The autoencoder architecture ensures the scalability of the compressor, allowing it to be trained using video data alone. In <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, it is pointed out that the average pooling demonstrates superior performance than the convolution-based compressor. In this work, we show that the convolution-based compressor with autoencoder pretraining significantly outperform the average pooling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To be specific, the compressor model <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> removes redundant information among tokens by compressing raw video features <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> to a compact latent space,</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=\mathcal{C}(f),\quad h\in\mathcal{R}^{t\times h\times w\times c}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=\mathcal{C}(f),\quad h\in\mathcal{R}^{t\times h\times w\times c}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> are the temporal length, height, and width of the feature tensor in the latent space, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\leq T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\leq T</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\leq H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\leq H</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w\leq W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w\leq W</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The decoder <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> model then reconstructs the raw feature representation from <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}=\mathcal{D}(h),\quad\hat{f}\in\mathcal{R}^{T\times H\times W\times C}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}=\mathcal{D}(h),\quad\hat{f}\in\mathcal{R}^{T\times H\times W\times C}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The compressor <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> and the video decoder <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> are trained together to minimize the difference between <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> using the mean absolute loss:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{rec}=|f-\hat{f}|\ =|\mathcal{E}(X)-\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{C}({\mathcal{E}}(X)))|" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{rec}=|f-\hat{f}|\ =|\mathcal{E}(X)-\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{C}({\mathcal{E}}(X)))|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Note that when optimizing <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> to minimize <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{rec}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{rec}</annotation></semantics></math>, the visual encoder <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> remains fixed. The loss forces the encoder to retrain all necessary information in the compressed representation during the compression process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The reconstruction loss also enables us to pre-train the compressor <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> using only video data, thereby learning valuable prior knowledge. In contrast, previous methods train the compressor alongside LLMs for next-text-token prediction tasks, which require costly visual-text pairs for training. The limited scale of such data may constrain the compressor’s performance.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">After pretraining, we leverage the compressor <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> with the visual encoder <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> to extract compressed video representation from the video, which is then combined with a text question <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> and fed into the LLM for response inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=LLM(P(\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}(X)),Q)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=LLM(P(\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}(X)),Q)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Residual Latent Space Constraint:</span> We empirically observe that aligning the compressor pretrained using Equation <a href="#S3.E8" title="Equation 8 ‣ 3.2.2 Autoencoder-based Video Compressor ‣ 3.2 Proposed Framework ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> with LLMs presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the lack of constraints within the compact latent space. Consequently, the learned compressor has limited generalization capabilities and may encode unseen data into gaps or ”holes” within the latent space, leading to a loss of meaningful representation. To mitigate this issue, we propose incorporating the average pooled feature of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> as constraints, redefining the latent feature <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> and reconstruction loss <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{rec}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{rec}</annotation></semantics></math> as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p12" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=\mathcal{C}(f)+avgpool_{3D}(X)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=\mathcal{C}(f)+avgpool_{3D}(X)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="S3.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{rec}=|\mathcal{E}(X)-\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{C}({\mathcal{E}}(X))+Avgpool_{3D}(X))|" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{rec}=|\mathcal{E}(X)-\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{C}({\mathcal{E}}(X))+Avgpool_{3D}(X))|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p13.1" class="ltx_p">With the proposed constraint, the compressor focuses on learning the residual (lost information) from the average pooling process, thus reducing the learning complexity of the autoencoder while implicitly ensuring that the learned feature <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}(f)</annotation></semantics></math> aligns with the same space as <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="avgpool_{3D}(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">avgpool_{3D}(X)</annotation></semantics></math>. Additionally, compared to Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), which enforce the latent feature space to follow a Gaussian distribution, our constraint achieves superior performance by eliminating nondeterministic behavior in the latent space, which can increase the challenges of learning for the autoencoder (see experiments for more results).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p14" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compression Ratio:</span> Compared with the setting where the output features from the visual encoder are used directly as input to the LLM (see equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.1 Preliminaries ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), the compressor reduces the token number by factors of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{T}{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mi>t</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{T}{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{H}{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>H</mi><mi>h</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{H}{h}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{W}{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>W</mi><mi>w</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{W}{w}</annotation></semantics></math> for the temporal, height, and width dimensions, respectively. This results in a total compression ratio of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{T}{t}\times\frac{H}{h}\times\frac{W}{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>T</mi><mi>t</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mi>H</mi><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mi>W</mi><mi>w</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{T}{t}\times\frac{H}{h}\times\frac{W}{w}</annotation></semantics></math> times.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p15" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Light-weight 3D convolutional kernel:</span>
We implement <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> using cascaded convolutional residual blocks. <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p15.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">We chose a convolution-based compressor for its simplicity and superior computational efficiency compared to transformer-based models such as Perceiver. Additionally, convolution operations effectively utilize the inductive bias that assumes that local visual tokens have high redundancy</span>. To reduce the parameter size, we decompose the 3D convolution operation into a 2D spatial convolution and a 1D temporal convolution. Additionally, we apply a channel-wise bottleneck mechanism when the 2D spatial convolution maps the feature to a lower dimension than the original, while the temporal convolution restores the feature to its original dimension. The downsampling is achieved through the convolutional strides <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s_{h},s_{w})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s_{h},s_{w})</annotation></semantics></math> for the 2D convolution and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> for the 1D convolution.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt a four-stage training recipe. (1) In the first stage, we train a VAE-based video compressor with supervision of construction loss. (2) Next, a projector between the video features and LLM is trained with our filtered ShutterStock data (<math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>3M) to align the visual features from visual space to language space. (3) In the third step, we unfreeze the LLM weights and further jointly train the LLM and projector with <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>8M data which is collected from subset of ShutterStock, Ego4D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, Breakfast <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, AVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, Vatex <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>, Something-somethingv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, Kinetics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> datasets. (4) In the last step, we finetune the model with our supervised finetuning (SFT) dataset which is collected from NextQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite>, CLEVRER <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite>, PerceptionTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, and Egoschema <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>. The SFT data adds up to 1M scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Benchmark and Metric</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct experiments on general general video understanding benchmarks covering a wide range of video lengths and video types, including:
<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PerceptionTest <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite></span> a multimodal benchmark designed to show perceptually interesting situations and defines multiple tasks. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> we report the accuracy of multichoice questions (MCQ).
<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ActivityNet-QA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>]</cite> contains 58,000 human-annotated QA pairs of 5,800 videos derived from the popular ActivityNet dataset. The dataset provides a benchmark for testing the performance of VideoQA models on spatio-temporal reasoning. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>, we report both accuracy and LLM based answer matching scores for above datasets.
The <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MVBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite></span> is a comprehensive Multi-modal Video understanding benchmark with videos ranging from 5s to 35s. MVBench covers 20 challenging video tasks that require a broad spectrum of temporal skills, ranging from perception to cognition. We return the average score on the downstream tracks as suggested by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. The <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">NExTQA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite> is a VideoQA benchmark that focuses on the reasoning of causal and temporal actions reasoning and object interactions understanding in daily activities. It contains 48K multi-choice questions with average duration of 44s. For these datasets, we report the multi-choice accuracy following previous practice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>.
For long video understanding, we choose <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EgoSchema</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> which is derived from Ego4D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, consists of over 5000 human-curated multiple choice question answer pairs, with videos of three-minute duration. And <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MLVU</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite> which is designed for very Long Video Understanding (LVU) tasks. It is constructed from a wide variety of long videos, with lengths ranging from 3 minutes to 2 hours. We report the mean accuracy of multi-choice accuracy on all downstream tasks as suggested by benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>SoTA Comparions</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with SoTA long-form video understanding methods.</span> First, we benchmark our method against previous long-form video understanding works on the EgoSchema, NextQA, and ActivityNetQA datasets, with results presented in the upper part of the Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Our method demonstrates significant performance improvements on all three benchmarks. Notably, our method outperforms VideoAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>, LLoVi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>, and VideoINSTA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> by 8.6% and 4.9% on the EgoSchema validation set and testing set. These multi-stage methods, which segment videos into short clips, extract clip captions, and aggregate objects through LLM, suffer from error propagation and information loss during multi-stage aggregation. In contrast, our approach learns to extract information end-to-end from videos. The Adaptive Video Sampler (AVS) efficiently filters out redundant temporal information, while our Spatiotemporal Video Compressor with AE maximally preserves of long-term spatiotemporal information, resulting in superior performance. Our method also outperforms LLaMA-VID and Movie-Chat on the ActivityNet-QA dataset by 4.8%. The two methods rely on conventional, complex pooling-based token compression strategies, such as LLaMA-VID’s Q-former-based compression and Movie-Chat’s memory-buffer approach for long-term information aggregation. In contrast, our method excels by providing a more lightweight yet effective solution, with less information loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with SoTA MLLMs.</span> Furthermore, we evaluate our method against state-of-the-art MLLMs across both general and long-form video understanding benchmarks in the lower part of the Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. For fair comparison, we focus on models using 7B LLM backbones.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Although we had access to only a subset of the Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) data used in previous works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, our model still achieves impressive results across all benchmarks.
Specifically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on three out of six benchmarks and comparable results on the remaining ones, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method.
Notably, our model processes EgoSchema and PerceptionTest using an average of just 1,440 visual tokens, substantially fewer than the approximately 6,000 tokens required by LLava-OV <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. This significant reduction in token usage demonstrates how our elegant design, incorporating the proposed sampler and compression module, achieves both computational efficiency and strong performance.</p>
</div>

<th id="S4.T3.3.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T3.3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Percevier</span></th>
