<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Ablation Study</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To validate our design choices and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed modules, we conducted ablation studies across four established long-form video benchmarks  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Video frame samplers.</span>
We evaluated our adaptive sampler against uniform sampling using an equal number of sampled frames, with results shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 SoTA Comparions ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. For videos without shot changes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, both sampling methods perform similarly; for example, on NExT-QA, where only 1% of the data contains shot changes, our adaptive sampling showed a modest improvement of 0.1%. This comparable performance is expected, as frames within the same scene tend to be visually similar. However, the adaptive sampler demonstrates notable advantages on longer videos containing shot changes, achieving a 1% improvement on MLVU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>. Further analysis of MLVU task-specific performance reveals significant improvements in tasks that heavily rely on key frames, such as anomaly detection, plot understanding, and needle-in-the-haystack scenarios. These results validate both the effectiveness of our proposed AVS and its robustness, maintaining strong performance even in videos without shot changes. In Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we demonstrate an example showing the different sampling results between uniform sampling and our AVS. As can be seen from the Fig <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, uniform sampling picks many similar video frames and waste the token budget while our AVS can pick the key frames that are not overlapped with each other and successfully localize the frame showing a women holding a phone.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17869v1/case_study_1.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/142;" width="685" height="142" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Examples of sampled frames using uniform sampling (top) compared to our AVS (bottom). AVS successfully locate the key frame to answer the question.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Video on Compressor.</span>
We first conduct the ablation study on our SVC design. We sample 32 frames as input and utilize the proposed SVC with a default compression ratio of 64× (4×4×4 for temporal, width, and height dimensions) across all ablations unless otherwise specified.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compressor Architecture.</span>
We evaluated our proposed SVC method against two baseline approaches: average pooling and Perceiver-based down sampling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, with results presented in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.2 SoTA Comparions ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Our AE-based method demonstrates superior performance compared to both baselines at the same compression ratio (64×), validating the effectiveness of our SVC approach for video information compression. Notably, our method outperforms average pooling even with half number of tokens which suggests that simply increasing the number of tokens doesn’t necessarily improve video representation. Rather, the key to effective video representation lies in eliminating redundant information while preserving essential spatial-temporal features. While the Perceiver approach achieves comparable performance to our method, it requires substantially more memory due to its cross-attention operations between queries and the numerous video tokens generated by the visual encoder.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T5.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T5.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T5.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Method</span></th>
<th id="S4.T5.3.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T5.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">EgoS.</span></th>
<th id="S4.T5.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T5.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">MLVU</span></th>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T6.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.T6.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">The effectiveness of different constraints in the autoencoder pretraining of SVC.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compression ratio.</span>
In Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 SoTA Comparions ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we analyze how different compression ratios affect benchmark performance. As expected, less aggressive compression yields better performance overall. However, when examining more aggressive compression scenarios, we discovered that spatial compression has a smaller negative impact on model performance compared to temporal compression. This difference might be attributed to the auto-encoder loss function’s effectiveness in preserving spatial semantics during information compression. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that balanced spatial-temporal compression ratios perform better than the spatially or temporally heavy pooling approaches under the same total compression ratio. For instance, a balanced 4<math id="S4.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>4<math id="S4.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>4 compression strategy significantly outperforms the more asymmetric 1<math id="S4.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>4<math id="S4.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>4 configuration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AE pre-training.</span> We show that the autoencoder-based pre-training is necessary and critical for the compressor. As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, AE pre-training consistently leads to 2%-4% performance boosts on all benchmarks. it is worth mentioning that training the AE with long-form videos that has shot changes is critical.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Latent space constraint.</span> We investigate the impact of different constraints on the latent space of autoencoders (AE) during pre-training, and results are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. Initially, we observed that when the compressor is pre-trained without any constraints, there are significant spikes in training loss, leading to feature alignment failure with LLMs. This result arises because the absence of constraints limits the generalization of the learnable compressor, potentially causing it to encode unseen data into gaps or ”holes” in the encoder’s feature space, resulting in a loss of meaningful representation. Introducing Gaussian distribution constraints on the latent space, as in VAE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, partially resolves the issue but still yields suboptimal results. One possible reason for this is the increased difficulty in learning feature representations due to the inherent nondeterminism of the features. In contrast, our proposed residual constraints demonstrate superior performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we present a novel advancement in video representation learning through our novel dual-component approach. The proposed adaptive video sampler effectively reduces spatial and temporal redundancies by leveraging contextual information, while our VAE-based spatiotemporal video compressor further optimizes video features without significant information loss. The experimental results across multiple video benchmarks demonstrate that our method not only achieves state-of-the-art performance, but also provides a more efficient solution for long-form video understanding. This work opens up new possibilities for processing and analyzing long video content in resource-constrained environments, marking an important step forward in the field of video understanding with large multimodal models. Future work could explore the adaptation of our method to real-time applications and investigate its potential in other multimedia domains.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Implementation Details</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>MLLM Architecture</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the ViT-G/14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> pre-trained in the CLIP style <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> as the visual encoder to extract visual token features from sampled frames. The extracted features are subsequently passed to the pre-trained compressor for feature compression. The compressed features are then mapped into the LLM input space using an 2-layers MLP projector <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. Following the Llava-OneVision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, we employ QwenV2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> as our LLM.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Adaptive Frame Sampler</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we employ TransNet V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite> as the shot boundary detector due to its superior performance and efficiency, enabling real-time processing. Frames are sampled at 10 FPS as input to TransNet V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>. We set the window size for the non-maximum suppression algorithm to 3 seconds.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17869v1/case_study_3.png" id="A1.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/144;" width="685" height="144" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="A1.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Examples of sampled frames using uniform sampling (top row) compared to our AVS (bottom row). AVS successfully locates the key frame to answer the question.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A1.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17869v1/case_study_4.png" id="A1.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/142;" width="685" height="142" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="A1.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Examples of sampled frames using uniform sampling (top row) compared to our AVS (bottom row). AVS successfully locates the key frame to answer the question.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Compressor and Decoder Architecture</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The design of our compressor primarily follows the architecture of state-of-the-art (Variable-)autoencoders for images <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and videos <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite>. To reduce the parameter size of the compressor, we decompose 3D convolutions into 2D spatial and 1D temporal convolutions, and incorporate bottleneck connections between them.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To be specific, the compressor consists of cascaded <span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">residual blocks</span>, where each residual block comprises two <span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">convolutional blocks</span>. Each convolutional block contains a spatial 2D convolutional layer, followed by a 1D temporal convolution and a SiLU activation function. We avoid using 3D convolutions since they introduce a higher number of parameters. The 2D convolutional layer and the 1D temporal convolution are connected in a bottleneck fashion to reduce parameter size: the 2D convolutional layer outputs features with a dimensionality of <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d/4</annotation></semantics></math>, while the temporal compression maps the features back to dimensionality <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> represents the dimensionality of the features extracted from the visual encoder. Downsampling is achieved by applying a convolutional stride of 2 in the first convolutional block. Our <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4\times 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> compressor configuration contains three such residual blocks, where the first two blocks perform downsampling, and the overall structure has approximately 65 million parameters.
For the decoder, it follows a symmetric architecture to the encoder, with upsampling operations follow those used in VQGAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T7" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A1.T7.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A1.T7.3.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T7.3.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">Training Statge</td>

</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Training Setting</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Data Mixture:</span> The details of the training data used at different training stages are provided in Table <a href="#A1.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ A.3 Compressor and Decoder Architecture ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.
<span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MLLM training</span>
We train our model on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with a batch size of 512. The training process is divided into three stages. In the stage-1, we train the MLP projector to align the compressed visual tokens with the LLM input space. We keep the LLM, visual encoder, and compressor frozen. The model is optimized by using the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>. In the stage-2, we train MLLM to learn new visual knowledge. The LLM and the projector are jointly trained with a AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> with a learning rate of <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>. In the SFT stage, we fine-tune the MLLM to solve various video understanding tasks and align with human preferences using our SFT data. We train the LLM and the projector with a AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> with a learning rate of <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">We use 32 frames as input for both training and inference. For the ablation study, the model is trained only during stage 1 and the SFT stage to reduce computational costs. When comparing our method to state-of-the-art approaches (Table 1 in the main paper), the model is trained across stage 1, stage 2, and the SFT stage.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compressor pretraining</span> We pre-train our compressor on the Stage 2 training data for one epoch, using a batch size of 512. We use the AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> with a learning rate of <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> to optimize the model. Note that the visual encoder is kept frozen.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional Experiment Results</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Comparison of Video Frame Samplers</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A.2 Adaptive Frame Sampler ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ A.2 Adaptive Frame Sampler ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Compact Video Representations for Efficient Long-form Video Understanding in Large Multimodal Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we additionally present the results of uniform sampling and our Adaptive Video Sampler. Consistent with our observations in the main paper, uniform sampling selects many redundant video frames, inefficiently utilizing the token budget. In contrast, our AVS effectively samples diverse key frames, accurately capturing the frame relevant to the questions “Who is decorating the Christmas tree outdoors in the video?” and “Where are the people tourists walking?” These results further demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed AVS approach.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
